title: Breaking the Silence Around Women's Health

contentHtml:
Presented by Narayana Hospital Howrah and supported by Prismaa Salon, the Pink Party brought together doctors, survivors and women from different walks of life to encourage early detection, challenge stigma and put women's health at the centre of everyday conversationsA woman's relationship with her body changes through the many chapters of her life, from puberty and motherhood to menopause and beyond. Yet, conversations around women's health, particularly breast health, often remain clouded by embarrassment, hesitation and silence. Unusual symptoms are dismissed, medical consultations postponed and discomfort endured, sometimes because women find it difficult to speak openly about their bodies.

Advt

It was this silence that the Pink Party, presented by Narayana Hospital Howrah and supported by Prismaa Salon, sought to challenge. Bringing together medical professionals, women achievers and a breast cancer survivor, the evening turned an important health conversation into an occasion for solidarity, shared experiences and renewed awareness.The gathering began with a welcome address, followed by the ceremonial lighting of the lamp by Meenulochani Annadurai, breast oncologist and oncoplastic surgeon, Narayana Hospital, Howrah; Suman Mallik clinical director and senior consultant, Radiation oncology, Narayana Hospital, Howrah; Monidipa Mondal, senior consultant Radiation Oncology, Narayana Hospital, Howrah and actor, dancer and theatre personality Jaya Seal Ghosh. The message was clear: breast cancer awareness must move beyond an annual campaign and become part of everyday conversations.

From ribbon to revolutionThe pink ribbon, now recognised internationally as a symbol of breast cancer awareness, has its roots in an act of grassroots advocacy. In 1991, Charlotte Haley began distributing peach-coloured ribbons to draw attention to inadequate funding for cancer prevention. Her initiative helped inspire the pink ribbon campaign popularised by Alexandra Penney and Evelyn Lauder in 1992.

More than three decades later, the ribbon continues to represent the need to make women's health visible and encourage early diagnosis.The evening also explored an unusual cultural reference through Raphael's La Fornarina, a Renaissance portrait traditionally believed to depict Margherita Luti, the artist's lover. Some interpretations have suggested that the woman's left breast may show signs of a tumour, although this reading remains debated. The discussion offered a reminder that women's health concerns have existed for centuries, even when society lacked the language or willingness to address them.

Advt

Awareness into actionAddressing the gathering, Suman Mallik, felicitated by The Times of India, called for a more sustained approach to breast cancer awareness."Breast cancer awareness is not merely a pink party but a pink revolution," he emphasised, drawing attention to the rising burden of the disease in India and the importance of recognising it at an early stage.

The discussion highlighted how delays in identifying symptoms, accessing medical advice and beginning treatment continue to affect outcomes. Awareness, the speakers stressed, must also reach communities where financial constraints, social stigma and limited access to diagnostic facilities remain barriers.

Advt

The message was simple: recognising a change, asking questions and seeking medical advice promptly can make a difference.Know your bodyOne of the evening's most engaging sessions came from Meenulochani Annadurai, who used everyday analogies to explain the importance of breast awareness.She pointed out that breast lumps can have several causes, including harmless fatty deposits and fluid-filled cysts. However, it is impossible to determine whether a lump is benign or cancerous through touch alone. Medical evaluation is essential.She also challenged the misconception that breast cancer is necessarily painful. A cancerous lump may not hurt, while pain by itself does not establish a cancer diagnosis.

Encouraging women to become familiar with their bodies, she compared breast awareness to the way grandparents instinctively notice even the smallest changes in their grandchildren. The objective, she explained, is to recognise what is normal for oneself and identify anything unusual.Changes worth discussing with a doctor include new lumps or thickening, alterations in breast size or shape, skin dimpling, nipple inversion, unusual discharge and swelling around the armpits or collarbone. Persistent itching, rashes or other unusual skin changes should also be evaluated. While women can use regular self-awareness as a way of noticing changes, it does not replace clinical examinations or mammography when recommended.The cost of waitingMonidipa Mondal, also felicitated by The Times of India, spoke about the importance of responding promptly to unusual bodily changes instead of allowing fear or social hesitation to delay medical consultations."Not every lump is cancerous, but only a physician can make that distinction," was the central message of her discussion.She also addressed the fear of losing a breast following diagnosis. Treatment, she explained, depends on the stage and characteristics of the disease. In suitable cases, medication can shrink a tumour before surgery, making breast-conserving procedures possible.The importance of appropriate screening was another key takeaway. Women should consult their doctors about screening schedules based on their age, family history and individual risk.The discussion also touched upon lifestyle choices, including adequate sleep, regular physical activity, balanced nutrition and healthier daily routines. While no particular diet or lifestyle can guarantee the prevention of breast cancer, maintaining overall health remains important.According to the International Agency for Research on Cancer's GLOBOCAN 2022 estimates, India recorded approximately 1.92 lakh new breast cancer cases among women that year, making it the country's most commonly diagnosed cancer among women.Survivors, stories and strengthHira Prasad, former principal of Birla High School, Mukundapur, shared her breast cancer diagnosis in 2023 and the determination that carried her through surgery and chemotherapy. Recalling how she chose to shave her head rather than wait for chemotherapy-induced hair loss, she spoke about embracing her changing appearance with confidence. A young student's innocent compliment, calling her beautiful despite her bandana, became a moment she continues to cherish. "Femininity is not defined by breasts or hair, so please come forward with your issues," she urged.Another survivor's account came from Rimi Ananya Mehra, who had Ductal Carcinoma In Situ (DCIS), an early, non-invasive form of breast cancer. A routine mammogram in London in 2023 detected the condition, following which she underwent surgery and radiotherapy. Having also lost her father to cancer and seen her sister battle breast cancer, Mehra has dedicated herself to raising awareness through the Cancer Fight Foundation, which she co-founded after returning to India. Her message was that sharing personal journeys can help others recognise the importance of screening, early detection and timely treatment.Making health a conversationActor Jaya Seal Ghosh brought a personal perspective to the gathering, appreciating the initiative for creating a space where women could discuss breast cancer without treating it as a taboo. "I like the name party because I think breast cancer is not a taboo. It is a cause which we can cure. This awareness that they want to create here is a wonderful initiative by Calcutta Times," she said.Drawing attention to how women often prioritise their families and responsibilities at the expense of their own health, she urged them to pay closer attention to their bodies and seek medical advice when something seemed unusual.She also recalled the experience of her former hairdresser who was diagnosed with breast cancer at a late stage despite having noticed something unusual earlier. The experience reinforced the importance of acting on symptoms rather than postponing medical consultations.As the evening drew to a close, the Pink Party proved to be more than an awareness initiative; it was a celebration of solidarity, learning and shared experiences. Women from different walks of life came together over interactive activities, including word tambola and a game that involved identifying marbles hidden in a sand-filled fishbowl, symbolically recreating the experience of feeling for lumps during breast self-examination. By turning an important health lesson into an engaging, participatory experience, the evening made its message all the more memorable.The pink ribbon may have begun as a symbol of advocacy, but its meaning today extends far beyond awareness campaigns. It stands for every woman's right to understand her body, speak without hesitation, seek timely medical attention and make her health a priority.Disclaimer: The above content is non-editorial, and TIL hereby disclaims any and all warranties, expressed or implied, relating to it, and does not guarantee, vouch for or necessarily endorse any of the content.
